newsitem.title: MEXICO: Salinas vows to return to Mexico but not politics.
newsitem.headline: Salinas vows to return to Mexico but not politics.

text.p: Vowing to return one day to Mexico, former President Carlos Salinas said in an interview published on Friday that he did not intend going back to active politics.

Salinas, who lives in self-imposed exile in Ireland, fled Mexico in March 1995 after his elder brother was arrested and jailed on charges of allegedly ordering the murder of the ruling party's secretary general, Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu, his former brother-in-law.
"It is not exile, nor do I want to stay abroad all the time. I will return to Mexico," Salinas said in the third and final part of a wide-ranging interview with the daily Reforma.

"I am not thinking about returning to active politics out of respect for the unwritten rule of distance of a former president, above all, respect for his successor," Salinas said in the interview conducted in Boston.
He travels often to the United States to visit his old school, Harvard University, and to attend meetings of the Dow Jones & Co. Inc. board.
Mexican presidents, all-powerful in office, traditionally keep low public profiles once they hand over the reins to their hand-picked successors.
But many Mexicans want Salinas brought back to the country to be questioned about his administration.

Critics allege Salinas was involved and holds key information to unsolved assassinations and blame him for leaving the country's finances on a knife edge which forced President Ernesto Zedillo's government to devalue the peso in his first month in office.
Salinas has always denied any involvement in the murders, including the March 1994 slaying of presidential candidiate Luis Donaldo Colosio.
He also rejected blame for the bungled devaluation which led to the country's worst recession in decades, on the grounds it happened after he left power.
In the interview, Salinas said his administration was committed to avoiding a sharp devaluation of the peso, a problem Mexico had often suffered under previous presidents prior to his 1988-94 reign.
"In November 1988, when I invited Pedro Aspe to be Finance Minister I told him: 'Your responsibility will be to avoid a brusque devaluation of the peso,'" Salinas said.
